latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Circulating hepatitis B viral antigens and antibodies can form immune complexes that deposit in medium-sized arterial walls and amplify complement-driven necrotizing arteritis. This mechanism is present only in the HBV-associated context, but it is central when HBsAg and HBV DNA are active.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Segmental transmural necrotizing arteritis of medium and small muscular arteries
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: The core PAN lesion is patchy transmural fibrinoid necrosis of medium and small muscular arteries, with lesions of different ages in adjacent arterial segments. It spares glomerular capillaries and pulmonary capillaritis, separating PAN from ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Segmental stenosis, thrombosis, and downstream ischemia
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Inflamed muscular arteries narrow, thrombose, and scar, causing tissue ischemia and infarction in kidney, bowel, nerves, skin, testes, heart, or CNS. The ischemic pattern is patchy and can be asynchronous across organs.

Fibrinoid destruction of arterial media weakens the vessel wall, producing renal, mesenteric, hepatic, splenic, or other visceral microaneurysms. Rupture can cause perirenal, retroperitoneal, intra-abdominal, or gastrointestinal hemorrhage.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Renal artery and intrarenal branch arteritis
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Arteritis of renal and intrarenal branch arteries causes renovascular hypertension, renal infarcts, hematuria, proteinuria, renal dysfunction, and aneurysm rupture. PAN renal disease is vascular and ischemic rather than crescentic glomerulonephritis.

Necrotizing arteritis of mesenteric, gastric, small-bowel, or colonic muscular arteries causes abdominal pain, ileus, ischemia, infarction, bleeding, and perforation. Severe GI involvement is one of the strongest acute mortality drivers in PAN.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Vasa nervorum arteritis with ischemic axonopathy
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Necrotizing arteritis of epineurial and vasa nervorum arteries causes painful asymmetric mononeuritis multiplex, sensory loss, wrist drop, foot drop, and slow axonal recovery.

Arteritis of dermal-subcutaneous muscular arteries causes livedo reticularis, palpable purpura, painful nodules, ulcers, and sharply demarcated ischemic skin necrosis. Skin involvement may be limited or a clue to systemic disease.

Arteritis of testicular or epididymal arteries causes acute orchialgia, orchitis-like presentation, focal hypoperfusion, and sometimes infarction or necrosis. Pathologic involvement is common at autopsy, while symptomatic infarction is uncommon but highly characteristic.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Systemic acute-phase and constitutional inflammatory activity
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: IL-6/TNF-driven systemic inflammation produces fever, malaise, weight loss, myalgia, arthralgia, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, anemia of inflammation, hypoalbuminemia, CRP elevation, and ESR elevation. It may precede organ ischemia by weeks to months.

PAN can involve coronary or myocardial muscular arteries, causing myocardial ischemia, infarction, arrhythmia, or heart failure. It is less frequent than renal, neurologic, skin, or GI disease but contributes materially to mortality.

High-dose glucocorticoids, cyclophosphamide, rituximab, and other immunosuppressants increase bacterial, viral, PJP, zoster, HBV reactivation, and wound infection hazards. Infection competes with vasculitis as a mortality pathway after induction begins.

Inflamed arterial segments narrow, thrombose, or heal with fibrous intimal thickening, producing downstream ischemia.
Transmural media destruction weakens branch arteries and produces microaneurysms that may rupture.
Renal arteries and intrarenal muscular branches are common targets of PAN.
Mesenteric muscular arteries are a major visceral vascular bed affected by PAN.
Patchy arteritis of vasa nervorum causes asymmetric ischemic nerve injury.
Dermal and subcutaneous muscular arteries can show the same necrotizing arteritis as visceral beds.
Testicular and epididymal arteries are muscular-artery targets and can become clinically ischemic.
Active arterial inflammation releases systemic cytokine signals that drive constitutional symptoms and acute-phase labs.
IL-6 is a major CRP driver in active PAN.
ESR rises with acute-phase proteins and anemia of inflammation.
Systemic cytokine activity produces fever or low-grade temperature elevation.
Recurrent or persistent fever is a common constitutional manifestation.
Active inflammation and steroid exposure can produce leukocytosis.
Inflammation and bleeding pathways can lower hemoglobin.
Reactive thrombocytosis often accompanies active systemic inflammation.
Inflammation and catabolic illness lower serum albumin.
Catabolic constitutional inflammation commonly causes several kilograms of weight loss.
Fatigue and malaise commonly precede organ-defining ischemia.
Diffuse myalgia and muscle tenderness are part of the PAN systemic syndrome and may coexist with muscle ischemia.
Renal ischemia activates RAAS and can cause severe or malignant hypertension.
Renovascular physiology frequently elevates diastolic pressure.
Systolic and diastolic hypertension raise mean arterial pressure.
Renal infarction, ischemic nephropathy, and hypertension-mediated injury can raise creatinine without crescentic GN.
Reduced renal perfusion and GFR raise BUN.
Renal ischemia, infarction, and aneurysm bleeding can produce hematuria despite the absence of primary glomerulonephritis.
Ischemic renal injury and hypertensive damage can cause non-nephritic proteinuria.
Occlusive arteritis of end arteries causes wedge-shaped renal infarcts.
Renal ischemia, hemorrhage, malignant hypertension, and contrast/procedural stress can precipitate AKI.
Angiographic microaneurysms are the visible structural correlate of weakened muscular artery walls.
Renal angiography often demonstrates multiple intrarenal branch microaneurysms in PAN.
Rupture of renal microaneurysms can cause sudden flank pain, perirenal hematoma, and hemorrhagic shock.
Any ruptured visceral aneurysm can produce major retroperitoneal, peritoneal, or GI bleeding.
Patchy stenoses, beading, and occlusions reflect active or healed arteritis.
Mesenteric ischemia commonly presents as abdominal pain, sometimes out of proportion to exam.
Flow limitation can be unmasked after meals.

Ischemic ulceration and ruptured visceral aneurysms can cause GI hemorrhage.

Retinal or optic nerve arterial ischemia can cause transient monocular visual loss.
PAN-related arterial thrombosis and hypertension can increase CNS ischemic event risk.

Diplopia can accompany ocular motor ischemia or CNS involvement, but is not specific for PAN.

Coronary arteritis or thrombosis can produce myocardial infarction.
Induction immunosuppression increases serious bacterial, viral, wound, and opportunistic infection hazards.

High HBV DNA sustains antigen load and immune-complex generation.
Severe GI ischemia, bleeding, or perforation is a major short-term mortality pathway.
Renal insufficiency, malignant hypertension, and renal hemorrhage increase acute and long-term mortality.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Both markers rise with acute-phase activity, though ESR lags and can remain high longer.
Renovascular physiology usually raises both systolic and diastolic pressure.
Imaging or surgical evidence of bowel ischemia indicates high infarction risk.
Transmural infarction can progress to perforation.
Bowel perforation causes peritonitis, sepsis, emergency surgery, and high mortality.
Severe GI bleeding can cause shock, transfusion need, surgery, and death.
Ruptured renal aneurysms cause perirenal or retroperitoneal hematoma.
Aneurysm rupture is a direct cause of major bleeding.
Major bleeding can produce shock or force high-risk intervention.
Severe renovascular hypertension increases CNS vascular event risk.
Serious infection is a major competing cause of death during induction therapy.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Active infection must be sought and treated because glucocorticoids can mask sepsis and worsen infection.
HBV-related PAN requires antiviral control and usually avoids prolonged uncontrolled immunosuppression.

failure_modes: HBV replication if antiviral therapy is absent
treatments.context_specific_role: Rapid suppression of active arteritis and constitutional inflammation; downstream organ salvage still depends on ischemic damage, aneurysm rupture risk, infection, and HBV context.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Pulse steroids can sharply worsen unrecognized infection and postoperative wound risk.

failure_modes: fixed infarct or necrosis does not reverse
treatments.context_specific_role: Short high-intensity anti-inflammatory push for rapidly progressive organ- or life-threatening active PAN; surgical or endovascular rescue is separate when tissue infarction or bleeding is already present.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Severe visceral PAN requires durable suppression of necrotizing arteritis in addition to steroids.
Dose adjustment and marrow monitoring are required with renal impairment.
Gonadotoxicity should trigger fertility counseling and alternative planning when feasible.

failure_modes: delayed onset relative to acute ischemia
treatments.context_specific_role: Cytotoxic induction for severe systemic PAN with renal, GI, neurologic, cardiac, or extensive cutaneous ischemic disease.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: HBV-associated PAN requires suppression of HBV replication to remove antigenic drive.

failure_modes: immune-complex arteritis persists until antigen load falls
antiviral resistance uncommon with current agents

side_effects.interpretation: tenofovir renal toxicity risk in susceptible patients

treatments.context_specific_role: Directly lowers HBV viremia and immune-complex antigen load in HBV-associated PAN and prevents reactivation during immunosuppression.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Plasma exchange is most biologically coherent when circulating HBV immune complexes are part of the driver.
Catheter placement and coagulation factor removal can matter during active bleeding.

failure_modes: rebound immune-complex formation if HBV replication continues
treatments.context_specific_role: Rapid removal of circulating immune complexes in HBV-associated PAN when combined with antiviral suppression and limited immunosuppression.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Anti-CD20 therapy can cause severe HBV reactivation without antiviral prophylaxis.

failure_modes: limited direct evidence in classic PAN
treatments.context_specific_role: B-cell-directed option for selected refractory or relapse contexts; HBV screening and prophylaxis are central.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Azathioprine has more pregnancy experience than methotrexate, mycophenolate, or cyclophosphamide.

treatments.context_specific_role: Steroid-sparing maintenance after remission or less aggressive non-life-threatening disease contexts.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Methotrexate accumulates in renal impairment and can cause severe marrow/mucosal toxicity.

failure_modes: not suitable for severe renal or GI-threatening PAN
treatments.context_specific_role: Steroid-sparing maintenance or non-severe disease option when renal function, liver tests, and pregnancy context allow.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Active extravasation or rapidly expanding hematoma requires mechanical control; immunosuppression alone is too slow.

treatments.context_specific_role: Mechanical rescue for ruptured or high-risk aneurysm/active bleeding while systemic immunosuppression controls the underlying arteritis.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Perforation or necrotic bowel requires source control; immunosuppression cannot reverse devitalized bowel.

failure_modes: new ischemic segments if vasculitis remains active

side_effects.interpretation: postoperative infection if wound/source not controlled

treatments.context_specific_role: Rescue for bowel necrosis, perforation, or uncontrolled intra-abdominal sepsis from PAN mesenteric disease.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: RAAS blockade can worsen GFR or potassium in advanced renal ischemia; calcium-channel blockers or beta blockers may be safer initially.

failure_modes: AKI or hyperkalemia with RAAS blockade
treatments.context_specific_role: Risk reduction for hypertensive kidney, CNS, cardiac, and aneurysm complications during and after vasculitis control.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Dialysis treats uremia, hyperkalemia, acidosis, or volume overload but does not treat arteritis.

failure_modes: does not restore infarcted renal tissue
treatments.context_specific_role: Organ support for severe PAN-associated renal ischemia, hemorrhage-associated AKI, or treatment/procedure-related renal failure.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: PJP prophylaxis matters most during high-dose steroid plus cyclophosphamide or rituximab exposure.

side_effects.interpretation: tubular secretion blockade or renal adverse effect

treatments.context_specific_role: PJP prophylaxis during high-risk induction immunosuppression.

middle_aged_or_older_adult.trajectory_modulation: Classic systemic PAN is more common in middle-aged and older adults and organ damage tolerance is lower.

pediatric_or_young_adult.trajectory_modulation: Early-onset PAN-like disease should raise DADA2 or monogenic vasculopathy context.

male.trajectory_modulation: Male predominance is modest; testicular manifestations only apply to male anatomy.

hbsag_positive_or_hbv_dna_detectable.trajectory_modulation: HBV-associated PAN is immune-complex driven and should not be modeled as ANCA vasculitis.

present_or_strongly_suspected.trajectory_modulation: DADA2 causes PAN-like medium-vessel vasculopathy with early strokes, livedo, systemic inflammation, and relapses; targeted TNF blockade is outside this PAN core treatment set but should be considered when confirmed.

bowel_ischemia_bleeding_or_perforation.trajectory_modulation: GI ischemia, bleeding, and perforation are major short-term mortality drivers.

present.trajectory_modulation: Renal insufficiency and severe hypertension raise acute organ risk and treatment toxicity.
Infection does not define PAN but strongly changes treatment hazard.

supportive_care: Screen HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs, HBV DNA, HCV, HIV, TB, and strongyloides before major immunosuppression when timing allows.
When HBV-associated PAN is present, start potent antiviral therapy and coordinate hepatology/rheumatology; monitor HBV DNA and transaminases during and after immunosuppression.

Map involved vascular beds with CTA/MRA/angiography when PAN is suspected and presentation suggests renal, mesenteric, hepatic, splenic, or other visceral arterial disease; keep angiographic microaneurysms as confirmatory/context evidence in case files.
Do not treat pulmonary capillaritis or crescentic glomerulonephritis as typical PAN manifestations; if present, evaluate ANCA-associated vasculitis, anti-GBM disease, SLE, infection, or overlap.
Urgent surgical consultation for peritonitis, bowel infarction, suspected perforation, or uncontrolled GI bleeding; immunosuppression cannot rescue devitalized bowel.
Urgent interventional radiology or vascular surgery for active aneurysm bleeding, expanding perirenal/retroperitoneal hematoma, or high-risk visceral aneurysm.
Aggressive blood pressure monitoring and control; monitor creatinine and potassium after RAAS blockade or contrast exposure.
Serial CBC, creatinine, urinalysis/protein quantification, CRP/ESR, liver enzymes, and symptom/vascular exam during induction and taper.
PJP prophylaxis during high-dose glucocorticoid plus cyclophosphamide or rituximab exposure; adjust for renal function and potassium.
Vaccination review before immunosuppression: influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19, recombinant zoster, and HBV vaccination when nonimmune and not acutely infected.
Bone protection, glucose monitoring, gastric protection in high-risk patients, mood/sleep monitoring, and infection education during high-dose glucocorticoids.
Cyclophosphamide safety bundle: mesna/hydration when appropriate, urinalysis for hematuria, CBC nadir monitoring, contraception, and fertility preservation counseling.
Neurology and rehabilitation for mononeuritis multiplex with foot drop, pain control, bracing, and physical/occupational therapy.
Wound care and infection surveillance for skin ulcers, necrosis, postoperative wounds, or stomas.

Patient education on urgent symptoms: new severe abdominal pain, hematemesis/melena, flank pain, syncope, focal neurologic deficit, chest pain, rapidly progressive neuropathy, testicular pain, or new necrotic skin lesions.
